episodes.title: Twelve Watts, and a Better Question
episodes.episodeSubtitle: Does a promising change help the task, the gut, and the person?
episodes.summary: Ying and Bing examine a small cycling trial of bicarbonate gel after prolonged riding, then connect its promise and limits with gastrointestinal measurement, supplement uncertainty, hypoxic sprinting, recovery therapy, sleep, school exercise, and alcohol craving. Their central question is what evidence would justify keeping a new strategy.
learningGoals: Interpret the cycling gel result within its population, comparison, task order, and uncertainty.
Separate symptom scores and physiological markers from meaningful functional outcomes.
Distinguish acute responses, long-term adaptations, exploratory findings, and mixed-design pooled estimates.
Describe a practical comparison process while recognizing that the EDGE SPORT workflow is unvalidated.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and I keep imagining a rider who's done everything carefully but still fades near the finish, wondering whether one more gel would help. This week we're asking what would make an added strategy worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'm Bing, and you're listening to edgeSport4Podcast, spoken as Edge Sport for Podcast. That rider's question feels familiar because a promising average can sound very personal, especially when the headline offers twelve extra watts after a long ride.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Exactly. But extra compared with what, and during which part of the ride?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Compared with the same carbohydrate intake without bicarbonate. Eleven trained cyclists completed both conditions in a randomized crossover experiment, so each person supplied their own comparison, and they were already accustomed to substantial carbohydrate intake during exercise.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That background matters. Both conditions provided eighty grams of carbohydrate per hour during three hours of riding, and the added gel supplied a specific bicarbonate formulation, so this tested an addition to established fueling rather than a rescue for inadequate carbohydrate.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And the performance test came after that riding, some short sprints, and a two minute effort. In the twelve minute test, average power was 239 watts with carbohydrate alone and 251 with the added bicarbonate, which sounds like a useful finish.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: The paired difference was twelve watts, with a confidence interval from three to twenty two watts. That's encouraging for this particular test, although both conditions remained below the unfatigued reference, so the gel didn't erase the effect of the preceding work.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So it helped one finish. Did the shorter efforts improve too?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: They didn't show a clear additional advantage. That keeps me from calling this a general power boost, and the fixed test order leaves another question open, because we can't separate prolonged riding tolerance from recovery after those preceding hard efforts or changes in pacing.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That's also where durability needs a careful definition. It's how well output holds up after accumulated exercise, while physiological resilience concerns things like efficiency and maximal oxygen uptake, so a better power result doesn't establish that every underlying physiological determinant was protected.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Right, and the blood buffering response doesn't give us a personal success threshold either. Bicarbonate and blood pH increased, but the bicarbonate increase wasn't significantly related to the performance gain, so would you call someone a nonresponder after one unsuccessful trial?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I wouldn't. Three of eleven didn't improve, but without repeatability data that isn't a stable personal label.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And even a real gain has to coexist with being able to eat and finish the task. Nobody reported severe or extreme gut symptoms under this study's definition, but these were familiarized riders with controlled diets, so how much reassurance should that give someone else?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Some reassurance about those conditions, not a general safety promise. The gut measurement review makes the wording especially important because it found fifty different scales across 126 studies, and ninety two percent of studies didn't explain why they chose their tool.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Those are study counts, not the percentage of athletes who had symptoms.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Yes, and two scales numbered zero to ten can still measure different things. Choosing a numbered category differs from marking a position on a continuous line, while changing the wording can shift the question from symptom severity to comfort, frequency, or interference.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Which means I'd want to hear what actually happened alongside the score. Did nausea appear at a particular feeding point, did the rider skip food, or did they slow down, because a combined total can hide those differences and lose the timing?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd keep the symptom names, anchors, and recording times consistent. The review isn't a formal systematic assessment of measurement properties, and limited reliability evidence doesn't amount to full validation, so it doesn't establish a universal score that tells everyone when symptoms become unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That makes a supplement ranking feel premature. How does the capsaicin review fit here?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: It asks a different question about single doses of capsaicin analogues, compounds related to capsaicin. The analysis combined twenty one crossover trials involving 348 adults across several performance domains, and its overall standardized effect was 0.20, with a confidence interval from 0.07 to 0.33.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: So that's a small average expressed on a common statistical scale, rather than watts or seconds. The prediction interval ran from negative 0.36 to positive 0.77, which allows quite different results across study settings, including settings without benefit despite that positive average.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And the authors rated overall certainty very low. Would a plausible mechanism change your recommendation?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: It would make the question interesting, but it wouldn't repair the evidence. Proposed pathways involving a receptor called TRPV1, calcium handling, and discomfort weren't directly tested in most trials, and adverse effects weren't assessed systematically enough to turn a dose curve into a safety guide.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Then I'd want stronger task specific trials and better tolerance reporting before routine use. The predominantly male samples also limit interpretation for women, and different compounds can't be assumed equivalent, so this review and the cycling trial don't let us choose a winning supplement.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Agreed. The same temptation appears in training when a bigger stimulus sounds automatically better.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The low oxygen sprint study gives that temptation something concrete to work against. Sixteen highly trained sprinters completed seven cycling sprints lasting either ten or fifteen seconds, with thirty seconds of rest in both conditions, and the longer sprints produced lower average power.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Across the seven sprints, average power was 6.85 watts per kilogram for ten seconds and 6.30 for fifteen seconds. That tells us about output rate rather than proving lower total mechanical work, and the longer condition also showed a greater decline across repetitions.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Yet average heart rate wasn't clearly different, while oxygen saturation measured shortly after each sprint was lower in the longer condition. So heart rate alone misses part of this comparison, and without a normal oxygen condition or long-term follow-up we can't declare the better training program.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Exactly. And a recovery marker can miss the outcome we care about too.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: You're thinking of CRET, the capacitive resistive electric transfer treatment added to massage. Twenty five athletes completed active and sham conditions after repeated hard cycling efforts, and because both conditions included massage, the comparison isolates the addition of active treatment rather than the value of massage itself.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Yes. At sixty minutes, lactate was lower with active treatment by 0.70 millimoles per liter, with a reported confidence interval from 0.05 to 1.50, but does that justify saying the athletes had recovered faster or were ready for more work?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: No. Strength, perceived fatigue, and next day's cycling performance didn't show clear advantages.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: There were some ultrasound differences too, but those didn't directly measure tissue repair or glycogen restoration. I find the contrast with the gel trial helpful because better twelve minute output there accompanied higher postexercise lactate, so the direction of lactate alone doesn't settle performance or recovery.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That makes me cautious about another shortcut, using a sleep questionnaire as a readiness verdict. In the exploratory analysis of 104 healthy adults, participants completed a demanding cognitive task or watched a neutral documentary before testing, while sleep quality and chronotype were examined as possible modifiers.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And chronotype means someone's tendency toward earlier or later timing. There were some general differences in reported mental fatigue and sleepiness, but those aren't the same as differences in the response to the cognitive task, so did the analysis establish that sleep doesn't matter?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: It didn't. Most analyses found no clear modifying effect, but a continuous sleep score analysis showed a small cognitive signal, and testing conditions may have limited sleep differences, so I'd record sleep, mental fatigue, and sleepiness separately rather than dismissing what someone reports.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That separation matters beyond adult testing. Can school fitness gains tell us how children feel?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Not automatically. The Danish FIT FIRST 20 trial randomized thirty schools and followed a high intensity multisport program for about forty weeks, but the denominators deserve care because 1652 children were randomized while 1195 with parental consent entered the analysis.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: The program involved three forty minute sessions each week compared with usual physical education. The adjusted additional gain on a repeated shuttle running test was 54.90 meters, with a confidence interval from 8.35 to 101.40, so that's an advantage over the comparison group's change.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Exactly, rather than simply how far the program group improved. Jumping and agility also favored the program, but psychological outcomes didn't show a distinctive benefit, and frequency, content, and intensity changed together, so schools can't identify one winning ingredient or assume fitness gains establish psychological gains.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Which brings us to a study where the reported endpoint actually was subjective, alcohol craving after brief exercise. Six articles suggested a short-term reduction, but the review combined controlled comparisons, before and after results, and natural activity observations, so what should we make of its pooled number?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Carefully. It reported an approximate standardized effect of 0.55, with an approximate confidence interval from 0.40 to 0.80, but that's neither a percentage reduction in drinking nor a clean estimate from comparable randomized trials, and the claimed young adult focus doesn't match several middle-aged samples.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: So a short-term craving signal doesn't establish sustained drinking reduction or relapse prevention.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Right, and it doesn't establish exercise as a way to manage withdrawal. It could inform discussion of an activity option within professional care, but I'd want clearer populations, consistent comparisons, and actual drinking outcomes before making a stronger claim about who benefits or for how long.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That returns us to our rider, because the useful question is what would change a decision. Our EDGE SPORT proposal is to choose the relevant fatigued task beforehand, keep the existing fueling background comparable, and record output alongside individual symptoms, actual intake, and willingness to continue.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd add repeated observations and the inconvenient results too, including trials with no gain or more discomfort. That's an unvalidated operational proposal rather than a tested package, but it makes the next discussion more concrete, especially if equipment, prior work, timing, or expectations differed.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Then keep a strategy only when comparable observations support the person's goal and its burden is acceptable. If symptoms interfere with fueling or completion, pause the addition and review it with the team, because these studies don't supply a universal dose, success margin, or symptom cutoff.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And don't let a reassuring heart rate, lower lactate, or better image make that decision alone. Read the written weekly report and original sources for methods and limitations, then bring the specific task and your actual experience into the conversation, because twelve watts is an invitation to investigate.

factCheck.claim: Eleven trained cyclists compared the same 80 g/h carbohydrate background with and without a specific bicarbonate gel during 180 minutes of riding.
factCheck.boundary: Randomized crossover experiment with incomplete blinding. Participants were accustomed to high carbohydrate intake. The exposure is a study protocol, not a universal prescription.

factCheck.claim: Fatigued twelve minute power averaged 239 W with carbohydrate and 251 W with added bicarbonate. The paired difference was 12 W with 95% CI 3–22 W.
factCheck.boundary: Testing followed three hours of riding and preceding short high intensity tasks. Both conditions remained below the unfatigued reference. Shorter tasks did not show a clear additional advantage.

factCheck.claim: Three of eleven cyclists did not improve twelve minute performance. Bicarbonate increases were not significantly correlated with performance improvement.
factCheck.boundary: No protocol-specific repeatability evidence establishes stable individual responder classifications or a biochemical success threshold.

factCheck.claim: No participant reported severe or extreme gastrointestinal symptoms under the cycling trial's definition.
factCheck.boundary: Small familiarized sample with controlled diets and limited symptom-tool validation. This does not establish general safety or superiority over other formulations.

factCheck.claim: The gastrointestinal review included 126 studies using 50 scales. Ninety two percent did not explain tool selection.
factCheck.boundary: These are study-level descriptions, not symptom prevalence. The review was not a formal systematic assessment of measurement properties and established no universal severity cutoff.

factCheck.claim: The capsaicin analogue analysis included 21 crossover trials and 348 adults. Overall g was 0.20 with 95% CI 0.07–0.33 and prediction interval −0.36 to 0.77.
factCheck.boundary: Overall certainty was very low. Predominantly male samples, heterogeneous compounds and tasks, and incomplete adverse-effect assessment prevent routine recommendations, dose equivalence, or supplement rankings.

factCheck.claim: Sixteen highly trained sprinters completed seven ten or fifteen second cycling sprints in hypoxia with thirty seconds of rest. Average power was 6.85 and 6.30 W/kg respectively.
factCheck.boundary: Lower average power does not establish lower total mechanical work. The acute pilot study had no normoxic comparison or long-term adaptation follow-up.

factCheck.claim: Longer hypoxic sprints produced lower sampled post-sprint oxygen saturation without a clear average heart-rate difference.
factCheck.boundary: Oxygen saturation was sampled about ten seconds after each sprint, not continuously. The result establishes neither a universal stopping threshold nor an optimal training program.

factCheck.claim: In 25 athletes, active CRET added to massage lowered sixty minute lactate by a reported 0.70 mmol/L compared with sham plus massage, with 95% CI 0.05–1.50.
factCheck.boundary: Difference direction is sham minus active. Strength, perceived fatigue, and next-day Wingate performance showed no clear advantage. Absence of significance does not establish equivalence. Table and inference labels require editorial review.

factCheck.claim: The exploratory sleep analysis involved 104 healthy adults. Most analyses did not detect clear modification of the mental fatigue response, while continuous sleep scores showed a small cognitive signal.
factCheck.boundary: Secondary hypotheses were not preregistered and exploratory multiplicity was uncontrolled. General subjective differences differ from response interactions. Findings do not establish that sleep is unimportant.

factCheck.claim: The school trial randomized 1652 children across thirty schools and analyzed 1195 with parental consent. After about forty weeks, the adjusted additional shuttle-test gain was 54.90 m with 95% CI 8.35–101.40 m.
factCheck.boundary: The estimate is a group-by-time difference, not an intervention group's raw gain. Frequency, content, and intensity changed together. Psychological outcomes showed no intervention-specific advantage.

factCheck.claim: Six articles on brief exercise and alcohol craving reported approximate g 0.55 with approximate 95% CI 0.40–0.80.
factCheck.boundary: Mixed comparison structures and age inconsistencies limit interpretation. This is not a drinking reduction percentage or proof of withdrawal safety, sustained drinking reduction, or relapse prevention.

closingTakeaways: Match an added strategy to a specific task and a comparable existing fueling background.
Record individual symptoms, their timing, and interference with feeding or task completion.
Interpret heart rate, lactate, imaging, and questionnaires alongside actual function.
Repeated comparisons and joint review are an unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal, without universal doses or decision thresholds.
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for methods and limitations.

episodes.episodeSubtitle: Creatine, confidence after ACL reconstruction, and what a spine screening score can tell us
episodes.summary: Ying and Bing explore when a measurement should change a training decision. They discuss adult creatine trials, physiotherapists' experiences of psychological support after ACL reconstruction, and spine screening in adolescent rhythmic gymnasts, keeping average effects, professional experience, and screening associations distinct.
learningGoals: Interpret standardized strength effects without converting them into personal guarantees.
Distinguish lean mass, fat mass, and body fat percentage.
Explain what physiotherapist focus groups can contribute to ACL rehabilitation decisions.
Distinguish spine screening categories from diagnoses and causal evidence.
Identify what additional information could support maintaining training, progressing a task, or arranging professional assessment.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and imagine sitting with your coffee and a training report that looks better than last month's. Before you celebrate or change the plan, what does that improvement actually give you permission to do?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'm Bing, and here on edgeSport4Podcast we're asking when a change is enough to act on. This week's report brings together strength gains, confidence after knee reconstruction, and spine screening, with very different evidence behind each.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And the person looking at that report may want a simple answer. Should I keep going, try the next task, or get something checked? Our job today is to see which parts of those questions the research can actually answer.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Let's keep asking what was measured and whose experience it represents. That should make the practical answers more useful.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: The creatine paper gives us an actual intervention comparison. It pooled randomized trials of adults doing resistance training with creatine against adults doing resistance training with a placebo, so training was part of both sides of the comparison.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That matters when someone credits everything to the supplement. The authors reported 63 trials and 1,489 adults overall, but different outcomes used different subsets of studies, so we shouldn't add the outcome sample sizes together.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Before we give the strength result, what does the effect number mean for someone who usually thinks in kilograms?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: They used Hedges' g, which puts the difference in the groups' changes onto a standardized scale. That lets researchers combine different strength measurements, but a value of point five doesn't mean half a kilogram or a fifty percent improvement.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: On that scale, the upper body strength effect was point five four in favor of creatine. For lower body strength, the estimate was point five five after removing one outlying effect value, while the complete analysis gave point six six.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So the average favors adding creatine, and removing that unusual value made the lower body estimate smaller. How certain is that average?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: For that lower body estimate, the ninety five percent confidence interval ran from point three eight to point seven one. That's uncertainty around the estimated average effect, but a coach also needs to ask how much results might vary across study settings.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That's where the prediction interval helps. After removing the outlier, it ranged from minus point zero four to one point one four, crossing zero and leaving room for a future study setting with little or no benefit.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And that interval describes possible study effects, rather than giving an individual athlete their own predicted range of strength gains.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Exactly, and publication bias is another reason to stay measured. A sensitivity analysis that modeled potentially missing effects reduced both strength estimates, although they remained positive. Those modeled effects weren't additional trials that researchers had actually conducted.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: I still find the average strength signal useful for a nutrition discussion. But suppose someone says their scan shows more lean mass and less body fat percentage, so creatine must have built muscle and burned fat. Would you accept both claims?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd separate them. Lean mass increased on average, but lean mass includes water as well as other nonfat tissue, and this analysis couldn't separate those contributions. Calling all of that increase new muscle would go beyond the measurements.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And a smaller fat percentage can happen when the total changes, even without a clear reduction in the amount of fat?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Yes, that's the denominator changing. The analysis found a small decrease in body fat percentage but didn't detect a significant difference in fat mass, so it doesn't establish a fat loss benefit from adding creatine to training.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Then I'd want to know whether the person is getting stronger in a way they value and how they feel about any weight change. Can this paper at least tell us which supplement schedule is most likely to deliver that?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: It didn't identify consistent effects of dose or supplementation schedule on the results. That leaves the best prescription unresolved, and it doesn't establish that all schedules work equally well. The authors rated overall evidence certainty from low to moderate.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: So there's enough to discuss a possible addition, but not enough to promise a particular person's response.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And that discussion needs context. Women were less represented, diet and hydration reporting were incomplete, and the appendix wasn't available in the supplied evidence. For an individual decision, I'd want their training record, nutrition context, strength changes, and priorities alongside the average result.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Those priorities become especially visible when someone is rebuilding confidence after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, usually called ACL reconstruction. Our next paper asks how physiotherapists handle psychological challenges during rehabilitation, which is a different question from whether a treatment improves outcomes.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Different because we're listening to therapists describe their work, rather than following patients through a tested intervention?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Yes, there were 21 physiotherapists across six focus groups, with 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway. Researchers analyzed the discussions for themes, and there was no intervention comparison or patient follow-up measuring return to sport or reinjury.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: What I found useful was their description of a therapeutic alliance, meaning cooperation built around shared goals, agreed tasks, and trust. They described small achievable goals and gradually approaching feared movements as ways to connect physical progress with confidence.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Would you call those strategies effective based on these interviews, or would that skip a step in the evidence?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: It would skip the patient's experience and the outcome testing. These are strategies therapists described using, not demonstrated improvements in return rates, though they give us concrete questions about which task feels frightening and whether the athlete feels supported.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That last question feels easy to miss if the team believes it's already being supportive. The therapists also described group training as potentially helpful, but comparison with someone progressing faster could add pressure, so the same setting may be experienced differently.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Then a better confidence score wouldn't settle everything. What would you still want to hear from the athlete?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: I'd ask which activity now feels manageable and which still doesn't, as a practical application of the report. The therapists used psychological questionnaires inconsistently, and some relied more on conversation, so this study gives us no universal score that clears someone to progress.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd also ask whose timetable they're trying to meet. The interviews highlighted expectations from coaches, family, and teammates, along with limits in therapists' psychological training and access to referral services. Good intentions don't tell us whether needed support was actually available.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And we should resist turning every interview example into homework. Some therapists mentioned injury footage or returning to the injury location, but the study didn't establish when those approaches are appropriate or whether they're safe and effective.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Agreed. I'd use these findings to improve the conversation and clarify support needs, while keeping progression within the person's rehabilitation plan. I'd be more confident about prescribing a particular strategy if research included patient perspectives and measured patient outcomes.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That wish for information we don't yet have carries into the gymnastics paper. It compared spine screening results in 56 female rhythmic gymnasts and 302 girls of similar age who didn't participate in sport, using a single assessment rather than following changes over time.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Before the numbers, does a higher score mean more diagnosed scoliosis, or does it identify something that needs interpretation?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: It identifies screening risk. The Scoliosis Tele-Screening Test, or STS-Test, combines information such as family history, maturation, and visible asymmetry, so the total isn't simply a measure of spinal shape. This study didn't confirm scoliosis with imaging.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: With that distinction in place, the gymnasts averaged five point three four points, compared with three point four one in the comparison group. Those are points on the screening tool, and the group averages don't tell us each girl's classification.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Where did the difference show up when they looked at the categories instead of just the average score?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Mainly in the middle category. There were 35 gymnasts classified as medium risk out of 56, compared with 60 out of 302 in the comparison group. Keeping those denominators attached matters because the two groups were very different in size.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And the high risk category didn't show a statistically significant group difference, which doesn't establish that the groups were equal. It also means we shouldn't describe every risk category as elevated or turn the medium risk counts into numbers of diagnosed cases.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The training hours result is where I can imagine a coach wanting an immediate rule. Within the gymnast group, weekly hours and screening scores had a positive correlation of point four five six, meaning they tended to rise together.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: But we can't turn that association into an hourly ceiling, or assume reducing hours would lower the screening score.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Right, the study can't establish what came first or separate training from selection and other influences. The girls had at least five years of gymnastics experience and were in competitive tiers three and four, so this isn't a sample of everyone attending a gymnastics class.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Suppose a parent brings in a medium risk result and asks whether their daughter should stop training. I'd explain that the category needs clinical interpretation and isn't itself a stopping rule. What would help you make the next decision more concrete?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd want the components behind the score, the maturation and training context, and a clinician's assessment of what follow-up is appropriate. The authors suggested screening every six months during growth, but their study didn't test that interval or show that it prevents progression.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: There's also some editorial checking still needed. The paper's percentages don't fully match its category counts, and there are inconsistencies in statistical reporting, so we've retained the reported counts and means without quietly correcting the source.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That leaves a useful observation with a clear limit. To make stronger prevention decisions, we'd need follow-up connecting these screening results with later clinical outcomes, and evidence testing whether changes in training improve those outcomes.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: So here's our practical proposal from EDGE SPORT, and these studies haven't validated it as a combined process. Before changing training, write down what changed, what the measurement represents, what the athlete wants, and what unanswered question could change the decision.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd add a named person and a date for reviewing the next step. That makes maintaining training, trying an agreed task, or arranging assessment something the team can revisit, without pretending we've discovered a universal progression threshold.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: For this week, discuss creatine through actual strength goals and body changes, ask about specific fears during ACL rehabilitation, and take spine screening concerns to clinical interpretation. Each asks for a different kind of follow-up, and none supplies an automatic personal clearance.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And leave room for the athlete's answer to change the plan. You'll find the methods, numbers, and remaining uncertainties in the written weekly report and original sources. Thanks for joining us on edgeSport4Podcast, and we'll talk again next week.

factCheck.claim: The creatine review reported 63 randomized trials and 1,489 adults, comparing resistance training plus creatine with resistance training plus placebo.
factCheck.boundary: Outcome analyses use different study subsets with overlapping participants. Their sample sizes must not be added together. This is adult evidence, not an adolescent or ACL-specific supplementation protocol.

factCheck.claim: Upper body strength favored creatine with Hedges' g = 0.54, 95% CI 0.37–0.71. Lower body strength was g = 0.66 in the full analysis and g = 0.55 after excluding one outlying effect value.
factCheck.boundary: Hedges' g expresses standardized between-group differences in change, not kilograms or percentage improvement. Full and outlier-excluded estimates must remain distinguished.

factCheck.claim: The outlier-excluded lower body strength estimate had a 95% confidence interval of 0.38–0.71 and a 95% prediction interval of −0.04–1.14.
factCheck.boundary: The confidence interval concerns uncertainty in the average effect. The prediction interval concerns effects in future study settings and is not an individual prediction interval. Both upper and lower body strength prediction intervals crossed zero.

factCheck.claim: Publication-bias sensitivity analyses reduced strength estimates to g = 0.36 for upper body and g = 0.35 for lower body strength, with confidence intervals remaining above zero.
factCheck.boundary: Trim-and-fill models hypothetical missing effects rather than adding observed trials. This sensitivity analysis used a two-level method treating effects as independent.

factCheck.claim: Lean mass increased with g = 0.30, 95% CI 0.18–0.41. Fat mass showed no statistically significant difference, g = −0.10, 95% CI −0.23–0.03, while body fat percentage decreased slightly, g = −0.14, 95% CI −0.26–−0.02.
factCheck.boundary: Lean mass includes water, and the analysis could not separate water from tissue contributions. A reduced fat percentage does not establish fat loss. Standardized effects are not kilograms or percentage points.

factCheck.claim: The review did not identify consistent dose or supplementation-schedule moderation, and the authors rated overall certainty as low to moderate.
factCheck.boundary: Failure to detect moderation does not establish equivalent regimens or an optimal dose. Women were less represented, contextual reporting was incomplete, and the missing appendix prevents independent verification of detailed outcome-level GRADE assessments.

factCheck.claim: The ACL study involved 21 physiotherapists in six focus groups, including 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway.
factCheck.boundary: Participants were therapists recruited through professional networks, not patients. There was no intervention comparator or longitudinal patient outcome assessment.

factCheck.claim: Therapists described trust, shared goals, small milestones, gradual exposure to feared movements, mixed experiences of group training, external pressure, and referral barriers.
factCheck.boundary: These are professional accounts, not demonstrated improvements in return to sport, reinjury, or patient experience. The study validates no psychological clearance threshold and does not establish injury footage or injury-site visits as safe required tasks.

factCheck.claim: The gymnastics study compared 56 female rhythmic gymnasts with 302 similarly aged girls who did not participate in sport. Mean STS-Test scores were 5.34 ± 2.70 versus 3.41 ± 3.39 points.
factCheck.boundary: This was a single cross-sectional assessment without imaging-confirmed scoliosis. Gymnasts had at least five years of experience and were in tiers 3 and 4. Findings should not be generalized to all gymnastics participants.

factCheck.claim: Medium risk counts were 35 of 56 gymnasts and 60 of 302 controls. High risk counts were 2 and 16, respectively, with no statistically significant high risk category difference.
factCheck.boundary: Counts describe screening categories, not diagnosed cases. A nonsignificant difference does not establish equality. Reported gymnast percentages conflict with counts, so the script uses counts without deriving replacement percentages.

factCheck.claim: Weekly training hours correlated with STS-Test scores within the gymnast group, Spearman r = 0.456, P = 0.01.
factCheck.boundary: The association establishes neither causation nor a safe hourly limit. It does not show that reducing hours lowers scores or prevents disease.

factCheck.claim: The gymnastics authors suggested screening every six months during growth.
factCheck.boundary: The study did not test that interval, longitudinal progression, or the effectiveness of screening-linked interventions. Clinical interpretation is required rather than automatic training cessation based on a category.

closingTakeaways: Interpret creatine benefits alongside actual training, strength goals, and body changes.
Ask about specific feared tasks and perceived support during ACL rehabilitation.
Treat STS-Test results as screening information requiring interpretation, not diagnoses or automatic stopping rules.
Record the next step, responsible person, and review date as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and I'm thinking about that hopeful moment when someone says they're ready to do more, because this week's question is what would tell us their nutrition, training, and physical response can support that next step?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And I'm Bing. Here on edgeSport4Podcast, I'd like to stay with that moment before the calendar fills up, when an extra ride or a return to competition sounds appealing but we haven't quite agreed what success would look like.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That agreement matters because our three sources answer different questions. We've got cycling nutrition guidance built from narrative reviews, a randomized training and protein trial in women, and a retrospective series describing return to activity after combined hip surgery.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So before borrowing any number, we need to ask whether it's a recommendation, a comparison, or a description of what happened.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Exactly, and the cycling statement gives recommendations primarily for elite competitive cycling. It brings together fourteen topic reviews, so it offers a broad planning framework without a newly recruited sample or a single experiment proving the whole package works.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: For a rider planning a longer event, what would you want to know before discussing grams of carbohydrate?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: I'd want the duration, demands, and chances to eat or drink, along with what their stomach already tolerates. The statement treats terrain, rider roles, and food access as part of the nutrition problem, which makes the plan much more concrete.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Then the first comparison is event length. For cycling events lasting one to two and a half hours, the statement recommends thirty to sixty grams of carbohydrate per hour, with the actual arrangement shaped by that rider and that event.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And for events beyond two and a half hours, it gives ninety grams per hour. Those are planning recommendations with context attached, so how would you respond to a rider who wants to jump straight to what professionals reportedly consume?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd ask what benefit they're expecting, because the extra performance benefit of one hundred twenty grams per hour or more remains uncertain.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That's the useful challenge. Above sixty grams per hour, the statement discusses combining carbohydrates such as glucose and fructose that use different intestinal transport pathways, but that explanation still leaves us needing to rehearse the products and check actual tolerance.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And rehearsal includes whether the food is there when you need it. A target written on a training plan doesn't establish intake, especially when carrying capacity or opportunities to take a bottle constrain what the rider can actually do.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That gap also brings us to energy availability, meaning the dietary energy left after exercise expenditure, expressed relative to fat free mass. It describes energy available for other bodily functions, while carbohydrate availability asks whether fuel supply matches the particular task.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So adequate daily energy doesn't automatically tell us that carbohydrate is available around a demanding session. Is that the distinction?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Yes, timing and task still matter, and a single energy availability estimate can't diagnose relative energy deficiency in sport. The statement also gives a daily protein range of one point six to two point one grams per kilogram of body weight.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: With competitive cyclists as the main context, rather than everyone receiving that range automatically. It also favors responding to menstrual symptoms and individual experience over changing training or diet solely by cycle phase, which keeps the person's response in the conversation.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That population boundary becomes especially useful with our next paper. It studied women aged forty to seventy seven with little recent structured activity and low reported baseline protein intake, so we're moving into a different training and nutrition setting.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Different enough that we shouldn't call it a test of the cycling recommendations. What exactly were the women assigned to do?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: They were assigned to supervised resistance training three times weekly or that same prescribed resistance program followed immediately by cycling. Each training condition also had three assigned daily protein targets, making six groups followed over twelve weeks.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That added cycling is what the paper calls concurrent training, meaning resistance and endurance work in one program. But the extra exercise meant total training time and energy expenditure weren't matched, so this comparison includes the cost of doing more.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Right, and the prescribed resistance program doesn't prove the completed resistance stimulus was identical. Before the results, there's another constraint worth holding onto, because one hundred eight women were randomized but only eighty three completed the final assessment.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That's twenty three point one percent attrition. Do the reported comparisons include the women who dropped out?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: They don't, because this was a complete case analysis rather than a full intention to treat analysis. The missing outcomes could affect the comparison, and the report says baseline characteristics couldn't be compared between those who completed and those who withdrew.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Keeping that in view, the strength comparison favored resistance training alone. At week twelve, the baseline adjusted estimate of maximum leg press strength was six point six eight kilograms lower in the group assigned additional cycling, pooling the protein assignments.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Lower than the other group, which doesn't mean they lost that much strength. And maximum strength was estimated from repetitions.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Yes, that's a between group comparison. The cycling group's estimated maximum oxygen uptake was higher by four point five three milliliters per kilogram per minute, after baseline adjustment, so the apparent advantage changes when we change the outcome.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And oxygen uptake was estimated from heart rate responses during a submaximal cycling test, without directly measuring breathing gases. Since the additional training was also cycling, how much can we say about general fitness or the mechanism behind that difference?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: We can describe the test result, but can't separate added exercise, test familiarity, fatigue, recovery, and physiological adaptation. The study didn't directly measure molecular interference either, so it doesn't establish a biological explanation for the lower estimated leg press result.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Then a coach needs the person's priority before choosing between those outcomes. Did the trial show a difference in everyday function?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The thirty second sit to stand test didn't detect a difference between training conditions, and neither did the primary muscle mass estimate. That estimate came from bioelectrical impedance, which is affected by hydration, so we shouldn't turn it into confirmed muscle growth.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That leaves the protein question, and it's easy to see why people want a simple answer. The assigned daily targets were zero point eight, one point six, and two point two grams per kilogram, supported through dietary counseling during ordinary daily life.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: But counseling isn't controlled feeding. Did they establish actual intake well enough to say those amounts produce equivalent results?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: No, although reported group averages were close to the assigned targets, intake was self reported and diets weren't matched for energy. The main analyses didn't detect overall protein assignment differences, but equivalence wasn't established and some sensitivity findings depended on the model.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So I wouldn't use this to declare the lowest target sufficient for everyone or the highest necessary. More complete follow up, stronger intake verification, and results in the population I'm advising would change how confidently I'd use it for a nutrition decision.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That same question about what a result really establishes follows us into the hip paper. This was a single center retrospective series after combined periacetabular osteotomy, a procedure that changes the socket's bony coverage, and hip arthroscopy addressing problems inside the joint.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And there wasn't a comparison group receiving either procedure alone or nonsurgical care, so we can't use it to rank treatments. The encouraging finding was recorded return to preoperative sport or activity in ninety two of one hundred three hips.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Hips is the important word there. Those one hundred three hips came from eighty four people, not separate athletes.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Yes, the reported return proportion was eighty nine point three percent at the hip level. The analysis didn't clearly explain accounting for two hips belonging to the same person, so treating every hip as fully independent would overstate what we know.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And the recorded return matters to people, but what did returning mean here? The study confirmed sport or activity through records or later recall, without adequately establishing whether people regained their previous competitive level or sustained that performance over years.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: So someone can value being active again while still wanting an answer about competition. We can acknowledge the encouraging participation result and leave the performance question open, rather than making that person feel their remaining goal has already been measured.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Exactly, and time needs the same care. Among those who returned, the average was two hundred ninety seven point five days, with a standard deviation of one hundred eighty one point three days, describing considerable variation around that average.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That's a description of this group's experience. It doesn't give the next patient a clearance date or a deadline.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: And that experience includes further treatment, because fifty nine hips had painful fixation hardware removed. Twenty six people who couldn't be contacted were excluded, too, which leaves uncertainty about whether the observed return proportion represents everyone who might otherwise have been included.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd want both of those facts in a discussion of expectations. What about contact sport, because a player might hear that the study found no significant difference and assume their return prospects are the same as in noncontact sport?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: We'd need to slow that inference down. Return was recorded in thirty three of forty contact sport hips and fifty nine of sixty three noncontact sport hips, and the nonsignificant comparison doesn't establish equivalence or rule out an important difference.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: For a stronger treatment discussion, I'd want direct comparisons and longer tracking of competitive performance. For an individual's next activity step, this series leaves us needing the surgical and rehabilitation team's assessment, because it supplies no validated clearance test or universal progression schedule.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That brings me back to the hopeful person asking to do more. Our EDGE SPORT proposal is to write down the goal, actual training and intake, symptoms and functional response, and the next review, while recognizing that this workflow hasn't been validated by these studies.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I like having something we can revisit. What would actually change the plan when that next review comes around?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Under that proposal, we'd reconsider if food access or gut symptoms prevented planned fueling, or if extra cycling undermined the chosen strength goal. We'd check the actual exposure and measurement conditions before interpreting the change, with postoperative activity decisions staying with the treating team.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And we should let the person help choose what matters, because more cycling, a higher intake target, and a return record each leave something unanswered. I'd want us to agree beforehand which result would justify continuing and which would make us reconsider.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Then our practical recap is to fit fuel to the ride, count the added training, and keep return to activity separate from restored performance. Undetected differences don't establish equivalence, and our recording proposal gives the next conversation a starting point without supplying a universal threshold.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: That's a useful place to leave the coffee and open the notebook. You'll find the full comparisons and limitations in the written weekly report and original sources, and we hope your next discussion starts with what you're trying to achieve and what would support it.

factCheck.claim: The cycling statement integrates 14 narrative topic reviews and primarily addresses elite competitive cycling.
factCheck.boundary: It has no newly recruited intervention sample or unified effect estimate. Recommendation certainty varies by topic.

factCheck.claim: Recommended carbohydrate intake during cycling events is 30–60 g/hour for events lasting 1–2.5 hours and 90 g/hour for events longer than 2.5 hours.
factCheck.boundary: These are context-dependent recommendations requiring attention to access and gastrointestinal tolerance. Additional benefit from 120 g/hour or more remains uncertain.

factCheck.claim: The cycling statement recommends daily protein intake of 1.6–2.1 g/kg body weight.
factCheck.boundary: This is guidance primarily for competitive cyclists, not a new dose-response trial or a universal prescription for all populations.

factCheck.claim: Energy availability expresses dietary energy remaining after exercise expenditure relative to fat-free mass.
factCheck.boundary: One estimate cannot diagnose relative energy deficiency in sport. Adequate total energy does not establish appropriate carbohydrate availability for a specific session.

factCheck.claim: The cycling statement does not support universally changing training or diet solely according to menstrual cycle phase.
factCheck.boundary: Individual symptoms and responses remain relevant. This is not evidence that symptoms should be ignored.

factCheck.claim: The 12-week randomized trial assigned 108 women aged 40–77 to two training conditions and three protein targets. Eighty-three completed assessment, with 25 withdrawals representing 23.1% attrition.
factCheck.boundary: Analysis used complete cases rather than full intention to treat. Menopausal status and hormone therapy were not formally assessed.

factCheck.claim: Concurrent training added cycling immediately after the prescribed resistance program, performed three times weekly.
factCheck.boundary: Training time and energy expenditure were not matched. Incomplete reporting of completed training prevents confirmation of equal achieved resistance stimuli.

factCheck.claim: At week 12, the baseline-adjusted concurrent-training minus resistance-training difference in estimated leg press one-repetition maximum was −6.68 kg, with 95% CI −8.32 to −5.04.
factCheck.boundary: This pooled comparison across protein assignments is not a within-group strength loss. Strength was estimated from repetitions, and the result does not establish a molecular interference mechanism.

factCheck.claim: The adjusted concurrent-training minus resistance-training difference in estimated VO₂max was 4.53 mL/kg/min, with 95% CI 3.80–5.25.
factCheck.boundary: VO₂max was estimated with the submaximal Ekblom–Bak cycling test, not directly measured using respiratory gases. Confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

factCheck.claim: Training-condition differences were not detected for estimated skeletal muscle mass or 30-second sit-to-stand performance.
factCheck.boundary: Adjusted differences were −0.16 kg for BIA skeletal muscle mass, 95% CI −0.45 to 0.13, and 0.27 repetitions for sit-to-stand, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.67. Nondetection does not establish equivalence, and BIA does not confirm hypertrophy.

factCheck.claim: Assigned protein targets were 0.8, 1.6, and 2.2 g/kg/day. Main analyses did not detect overall protein-assignment differences.
factCheck.boundary: Intake was self-reported under dietary counseling, without controlled feeding or matched energy intake. Some sensitivity findings depended on the model, and complete supplementary tables were unavailable in the packet. Neither equivalence nor a universal minimum requirement was established.

factCheck.claim: The hip series recorded return to preoperative sport or activity in 92 of 103 hips, or 89.3%, from 84 patients.
factCheck.boundary: The denominator is hips, not independent athletes. This single-center retrospective series lacked a direct treatment comparator and did not clearly describe adjustment for correlation between two hips from one patient.

closingTakeaways: Match cycling fuel to the task, food access, and tolerance.
Count additional cycling as added exposure and judge outcomes against the person's goal.
Undetected protein differences do not establish equivalent doses or universal sufficiency.
Read hip return rates with their hip-level denominator, further procedures, and unknown competitive outcomes.
Record the goal, actual exposure, response, and reassessment plan as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal.
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for full methods and limitations.

Explain pitch-specific trends, within-game variability, and between-group slope differences.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Imagine you're watching a pitcher you know well. The fastball looks a little slower again, and afterward they say, 'I'm just not bouncing back the way I usually do.' That leaves a very human question: do we change something now, or are we reading too much into a number? I'm Ying, and this is edgeSport4Podcast.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And I'm Bing. I'd want to take that person seriously without making the graph sound like a diagnosis. This week's central question is how a team checks a persistent velocity decline, considers changes to pitching exposure, and starts an assessment. What evidence would actually change the next decision?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: We've got four sources: MLB pitching data, walking and mortality, lumbar and hamstring diagnoses, and a review of natural products, gut microbes, and fatigue. They don't test one shared intervention. Together, they give us different chances to practice the same editorial discipline: say what was measured, then keep the conclusion inside that boundary.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And let's keep two conversations visible. One is what the studies found. The other is what EDGE SPORT proposes a team could do with that information. A sensible workflow can still be untested. I'd hate for listeners to hear our practical suggestions and assume researchers have already shown that following them prevents shoulder surgery.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: The pitching study looked backward at 27 MLB pitchers who underwent their first shoulder capsulolabral repair, involving the shoulder capsule and labrum, and 54 matched controls. Matching included season, pitching role, throwing side, age, and pitch count. These were selected surgical cases, so this isn't a study of every possible reason a pitcher's shoulder might hurt.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The tracking dataset sounds enormous: 161,979 pitches across 3,347 appearances. But those pitches came from a small number of people. Repeated observations help describe each player's pattern; they don't turn the study into one with 161,979 independent athletes. Ying, what stood out when the researchers compared the groups over time?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: There were two different layers. In the previous season, the eventual surgical cases had higher average velocity for some fastballs and higher standardized spin overall. The more consistent velocity declines appeared later in the injury season and before injured-list placement. So a higher-output background and a recent downward trend are separate observations.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Let's slow down for the number that could easily become a dashboard alarm. In the final five appearances, the primary-fastball slope difference was minus 0.195 miles per hour per appearance, with a 95 percent confidence interval from minus 0.301 to minus 0.090. That analysis included 22 eligible cases and matched controls. What exactly is that difference comparing?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: It's the cases' rate of change minus the controls' rate of change. It isn't a claim that every injured pitcher lost exactly that much velocity each outing. And it isn't a personal removal threshold. The primary breaking ball also showed a more negative slope in cases, but neither result came with a validated individual prediction rule.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: There's also a timing problem. Injured-list placement gives the researchers a date, but it doesn't tell them when symptoms or tissue changes began. The decline could reflect a developing problem, fatigue, or other influences they couldn't separate. So calling this an early warning requires care: early relative to the list entry isn't necessarily early relative to the injury.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Another finding made me pause: cases had lower within-game variability in velocity and arm angle in pooled analyses. Here, variability means the standard deviation of individual pitches of the same type within a game. Bing, if a coach hears that consistent pitching was associated with surgical cases, should they encourage a less repeatable delivery?

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: No. That would turn an association into a treatment. The authors explicitly don't recommend deliberately increasing movement variability or reducing competitive output because of this finding. Statcast didn't measure tissue stress or muscle activation. Also, lower variation in arm angle doesn't mean a lower average arm angle. Those are different quantities, with different interpretations.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That's helpful. A player could have very similar velocities within each outing while their average velocity falls across outings. Consistency within a game and change between games can coexist. For a team, the useful question becomes whether comparable pitches show a persistent change, alongside what the pitcher reports about symptoms and recovery.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: And I'd need prospective evidence before trusting an automatic alert: how often does it correctly identify a problem, how often does it miss one, and does acting on it improve outcomes? This study doesn't answer those questions. No decline can't clear a shoulder, either. The direct evidence is from MLB, with uncertain transfer to youth, amateur, or postoperative pitchers.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Let's leave the mound for a walk. The next study asks about the combination of how much people step and how briskly they step. Its all-cause mortality analysis included 64,743 UK Biobank adults, averaging 61.5 years old, with 1,697 deaths over a median eight years. It followed observed activity; it didn't assign walking plans.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Activity came from seven days of wrist-worn monitoring. Daily steps describe accumulated stepping volume. The intensity measure, PK30, averages the day's 30 highest minute-level step rates, then averages across valid days. Those minutes don't have to be consecutive. So, Ying, someone taking a continuous half-hour walk isn't automatically doing the exact exposure measured here.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Right. And an ordinary average cadence on a watch isn't automatically PK30. The comparison group matters just as much: fewer than 5,000 daily steps, with PK30 at the overall fifth percentile, about 45 steps a minute. Every hazard ratio we're about to mention is relative to that joint reference, rather than a comparison with everyone else.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: With fewer than 5,000 steps and PK30 of 80, the all-cause mortality hazard ratio was 0.72, with a 95 percent interval of 0.54 to 0.97. At 5,000 to 7,500 steps and PK30 of 60, it was 0.70, interval 0.58 to 0.86. Different combinations showed lower hazards. Can we call those two routes equally effective?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: We can't. They weren't directly tested for equivalence, and nobody was randomized to either route. Another combination, 7,500 to 10,000 steps with PK30 around 100, had a hazard ratio of 0.57, interval 0.47 to 0.69. That's a relative hazard association during follow-up, not an individual's probability of dying or a guaranteed benefit from changing their routine.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The uncertainty isn't uniform, either. Under 5,000 steps with PK30 of 90 had an estimate of 0.64, but the interval ran from 0.32 to 1.32, crossing one. And an apparent upturn at the high end didn't persist across modeling approaches. We shouldn't turn that curve into a claim that more or faster walking causes harm.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: What would you take into a conversation with someone who finds step targets discouraging? I'd want to understand whether the obstacle is time, preference, or walking ability. These results make room to discuss volume and intensity together. But they don't provide a personal starting speed, a safe progression rate, or evidence that one watch's numbers match the research algorithm.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd use that opening, while remembering the measurement was one week representing years of follow-up. Unmeasured differences and undiagnosed illness could still influence the association. Steps also miss activities such as swimming and cycling. The practical gain is a more flexible conversation about activity, with the person's circumstances in view, rather than a newly mandatory number.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Our third study shifts from activity measurements to medical records. Researchers compared 1,269 people with a hamstring diagnosis with 1,269 demographically matched controls in one healthcare system. Ages ranged from 15 to 94. This was a general healthcare sample, which matters if we're tempted to tell a competitive sprinter that the percentages describe their situation.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Lumbar pathology appeared in 469 records in the hamstring group and 318 controls: reported as 37 percent and 25.1 percent. These were existing diagnostic or imaging records, including conditions such as disc degeneration or herniation. The study didn't establish which came first. Ying, is the takeaway simply to look at the back whenever a hamstring hurts?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: I'd phrase it more selectively. When posterior thigh symptoms recur or the local explanation doesn't fit, a clinician can consider lumbar history and assessment. Coexisting records don't establish where pain comes from. The study also didn't confirm every hamstring diagnosis with one uniform procedure, so we can't assume every record represented the same kind of structural injury.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The adjusted odds ratio was 1.84, accounting for age and body mass index, and the source didn't provide a confidence interval. Odds aren't the same as probability, so '84 percent more likely to develop lumbar disease' would be wrong. These are coexistence data, without a demonstrated sequence leading from one diagnosis to another.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: There's a detection issue too: people with hamstring symptoms might receive more lumbar investigations, making lumbar findings easier to discover. Some controls could have received care elsewhere. Bing, what would change your decision about further assessment here? I don't want the sensible idea of considering another symptom source to quietly become routine imaging for everyone.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd leave the imaging decision with the clinician's individual history and examination. The study didn't test whether routine imaging improves outcomes. It gives a reason to keep an explanation open, especially when the local picture is incomplete. It doesn't prove a lumbar cause, and it doesn't establish a preventive lumbar treatment for people with hamstring diagnoses.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: That brings us to fatigue, where a compelling explanation can feel especially welcome. The natural-products review included 26 studies: 25 in mice or rats and one in humans. The animal work mainly used exercise-to-exhaustion models. Because the studies differed substantially, the authors didn't pool them into a single effect estimate.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The proposed connection is interesting: products might alter gut microbes and their metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, with possible links to energy regulation, the gut barrier, and inflammation. But seeing microbes and fatigue measures change together doesn't prove that the microbial change produced the performance effect. Did any studies get closer to testing that connection?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Some animal experiments used antibiotics or fecal microbiota transfer to probe microbial involvement. That adds mechanistic support in those models. It doesn't establish the whole pathway in every study or show that an athlete will benefit. Even the directions of microbial changes weren't consistent enough to define one universal microbiome target.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: The human study involved matcha alongside resistance training in healthy, untrained young men. The review described lower subjective fatigue in week one, without an effect size or confidence interval. The eight-week leg-strength finding was described as a trend. That sounds like a reason for better human trials. What stops us from making even a modest product recommendation?

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: The thin human evidence, unclear sample-group reporting, and limited transfer to trained athletes all matter. We shouldn't reconstruct a total sample from ambiguous table entries or promote a strength trend into a clear benefit. This review can't rank products reliably, establish an athlete dosing plan, or tell us that a pitcher's persistent fatigue originates in the gut.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd change my confidence with clearer controlled human studies in relevant populations, reporting meaningful effects and uncertainty. For now, the mechanism remains a research question. A nutrition discussion can include any new products someone is using, but microbiome testing or a supplement shouldn't replace assessment of unexplained fatigue and declining performance on the strength of this review.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Let's return to our pitcher. From here, we're describing the EDGE SPORT workflow proposal in the weekly report, not an intervention the studies validated. First, check whether the signal is comparable: same pitch type, consistent units and measurement process, and a similar role or task. Keep training and game contexts identifiable, and mark missing data.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: I'd put the athlete's account beside that data immediately: symptoms, perceived recovery, pitch counts, and recent training. But I want to challenge the order slightly. If symptoms or worsening function make continued pitching questionable, data cleaning shouldn't delay professional assessment. Under the proposal, stop that session and involve the athletic training or medical team; existing medical restrictions take priority.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: Agreed. The spreadsheet doesn't get first refusal on care. If the team considers continued activity appropriate within limits, it can document an exposure adjustment and its reason. That might involve volume, intensity, density, or role. The report supplies no validated reduction percentage, rest duration, or velocity cutoff, so we shouldn't create one to make the plan look more complete.

transcript.speaker: cohost
transcript.text: Then make the next review concrete: who records the response, what changed, and what the team will reconsider before adding demands. The report proposes checking symptoms and recovery after activity and the next day. That timing is an operational suggestion. A single rebound in velocity doesn't establish recovery, and keeping good records doesn't prove the process prevents injury.

transcript.speaker: host
transcript.text: So my practical recap is: compare like with like, listen to the athlete, and use persistent change to open assessment. Keep alternative explanations available without assigning a diagnosis. Walking combinations can broaden an activity conversation; lumbar records can broaden a clinical question; gut mechanisms can guide research. None supplies a shortcut to an individual pitching decision.

transcript.speaker: cohost
