factCheck.claim: The pitching study included 27 MLB pitchers undergoing first capsulolabral repair and 54 matched controls, with 161,979 pitches across 3,347 appearances.
factCheck.boundary: Retrospective matched case-control data. Pitches are repeated observations from a small athlete sample, not independent participants; subgroup sample sizes differ.

factCheck.claim: In the last-five-appearance analysis with 22 eligible cases and matched controls, the primary-fastball slope difference was −0.195 mph per appearance, 95% CI −0.301 to −0.090.
factCheck.boundary: Case-minus-control slope difference, not each case's absolute decline or an individual diagnostic cutoff. Injured-list placement does not establish symptom onset. No validated prediction accuracy or intervention benefit was reported.

factCheck.claim: Cases showed lower within-game velocity and arm-angle variability in pooled analyses.
factCheck.boundary: Variability refers to within-game, same-pitch-type standard deviations. Lower arm-angle variability does not mean lower mean arm angle. The findings do not justify deliberately increasing movement variability.

factCheck.claim: The walking all-cause mortality analysis included 64,743 adults, mean age 61.5 years, and 1,697 deaths over median follow-up of 8.0 years.
factCheck.boundary: Prospective observational UK Biobank analysis using seven-day baseline wrist monitoring. The separate cardiovascular analysis used 70,075 participants and must not share the all-cause denominator.

factCheck.claim: PK30 averages the day's highest 30 minute-level cadences, which need not be consecutive, then averages across valid monitoring days.
factCheck.boundary: Not continuous brisk walking for 30 minutes, ordinary average cadence, or running-technique cadence. Direct comparison requires compatible measurement definitions.

factCheck.claim: Against fewer than 5,000 steps/day and PK30 at the overall fifth percentile, approximately 45 steps/minute, fewer than 5,000 steps with PK30 80 had HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54–0.97); 5,000–7,500 steps with PK30 60 had HR 0.70 (0.58–0.86).
factCheck.boundary: All-cause mortality associations against a shared reference, not randomized intervention effects or a direct equivalence test between the combinations.

factCheck.claim: At 7,500–10,000 steps/day and PK30 approximately 100 steps/minute, the all-cause mortality HR was 0.57 (95% CI 0.47–0.69).
factCheck.boundary: Relative hazard against the specified joint reference; not an individual absolute risk, guaranteed benefit, or optimal personal prescription.

factCheck.claim: Below 5,000 steps/day with PK30 90, the all-cause mortality HR was 0.64 (95% CI 0.32–1.32); high-end curve upturns were not consistent across models.
factCheck.boundary: The interval crosses one. Neither this estimate nor model-sensitive curve shapes establishes that more or faster walking causes harm.

factCheck.claim: Each lumbar/hamstring comparison group contained 1,269 people, aged 15–94. Lumbar pathology records occurred in 469 hamstring-group participants and 318 controls, reported as 37% versus 25.1%.
factCheck.boundary: General healthcare records, not an athlete-specific cohort or prospective incidence estimate. Temporal order, uniform diagnostic confirmation, and causal symptom origin were not established.

factCheck.claim: The age- and BMI-adjusted odds ratio linking hamstring diagnosis with lumbar pathology was 1.84; the source did not provide a confidence interval.
factCheck.boundary: An odds ratio cannot be restated as an 84% increase in disease probability. Detection bias and incomplete records remain possible; routine imaging benefit was not tested.

factCheck.claim: The natural-products review included 26 studies: 25 animal studies and one human study; heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis.
factCheck.boundary: Predominantly animal exhaustion models provide limited direct evidence for trained athletes. Some mechanistic experiments probed microbial involvement, but this does not establish clinical efficacy.

factCheck.claim: The human matcha study involved healthy untrained young men undertaking resistance training; lower subjective fatigue was described at week one without an effect size or confidence interval, and the eight-week leg-strength result was described as a trend.
factCheck.boundary: Ambiguous sample-group reporting does not support reconstructing a total sample. The findings do not establish a supplement prescription, product ranking, or clear strength benefit.

closingTakeaways: Check comparable pitch-specific data alongside symptoms, exposure, and recovery.
Use persistent changes to prompt assessment; no study supplies an individual injury or clearance threshold.
Interpret walking volume and intensity together without promising causal benefits.
Keep alternative symptom sources open without assuming lumbar causation or ordering routine imaging.
Require stronger human evidence before converting gut mechanisms into supplement recommendations.
Document adjustments and reassessment; the EDGE SPORT workflow remains unvalidated.
